danish.title: Tredje bog (1805) — Kapitel 3
paragraphs: Den gamle fyrst Nikolaj Bolkonskij modtog i november 1805 et brev fra fyrst Vasilij, der meddelte, at han og hans søn ville aflægge ham en visit. »Jeg er på vej ud på en inspektionsrejse og vil naturligvis ikke finde det ulejligt at tage halvfjerds ekstra mil for at besøge Dem, min ærede velgører,« skrev fyrst Vasilij. »Min søn Anatole ledsager mig på sin vej til hæren, så jeg håber, De vil tillade ham personligt at udtrykke den dybe respekt, som han, i sin fars fodspor, nærer for Dem.«
»Det ser ud til, at det ikke bliver nødvendigt at føre Marja ud i selskabslivet — bejlerne kommer af sig selv til os,« bemærkede den lille fyrstinde ubetænksomt, da hun hørte nyheden.
Fyrst Nikolaj rynkede brynene, men sagde intet.
Fjorten dage efter brevet kom fyrst Vasilijs tjenere en aften forud for ham, og han og hans søn ankom næste dag.

Den gamle Bolkonskij havde altid haft en ringe mening om fyrst Vasilijs karakter, og endnu mere i den seneste tid, da fyrst Vasilij under Paul og Alexanders regeringer var steget til høje stillinger og æresbevisninger. Og nu, ud fra antydningerne i brevet og fra den lille fyrstindes ord, så han, hvorfra vinden blæste, og hans lave mening blev til en følelse af foragtelig uvilje. Han fnøs, hver gang han omtalte ham. Den dag fyrst Vasilij skulle ankomme, var fyrst Bolkonskij i særdeles dårligt humør. Om det var, fordi fyrst Vasilij kom, eller om hans dårlige humør blot gjorde ham ekstra irriteret over besøget — han var i dårligt humør, og allerede om morgenen havde Tikhon rådet arkitekten til ikke at gå til fyrsten med sin rapport.
»Hører du, hvordan han går?« sagde Tikhon og henledte arkitektens opmærksomhed på lyden af fyrstens skridt. »Sætter hælen fladt — det ved vi nok, hvad betyder...«

Ikke desto mindre gik fyrsten klokken ni, i sin fløjlskappe med pelskrave og hue, ud til sin sædvanlige spadseretur. Det havde sneet dagen før, og stien til drivhuset, som fyrsten plejede at gå ad, var fejet: mærkerne efter kosten var stadig synlige i sneen, og en skovl var stukket ned i en af de bløde snedriver, der kantede stien på begge sider. Fyrsten gik gennem drivhusene, tjenestefolkenes kvarterer og udbygningerne, rynkende brynene og tavs.
»Kan en slæde komme igennem?« spurgte han sin forvalter, en ærværdig mand, der i manerer og udseende lignede sin herre, og som fulgte ham tilbage mod huset.
»Sneen er dyb. Jeg lader alléen feje, Deres nåde.«
Fyrsten bøjede hovedet og gik op mod terrassen. »Gud ske tak,« tænkte forvalteren, »stormen er drevet over!«
»Det ville have været svært at køre op, Deres nåde,« tilføjede han. »Jeg hørte, Deres nåde, at en minister kommer på besøg hos Deres nåde.«
Fyrsten vendte sig om mod forvalteren og fæstnede blikket på ham med rynkede bryn.

»Hvad? En minister? Hvilken minister? Hvem har givet ordre?« sagde han med sin skingre, hårde stemme. »Vejen er ikke fejet for prinsessen, min datter, men for en minister! For mig er der ingen ministre!«
»Deres nåde, jeg troede...«

»Du troede!« råbte fyrsten, og hans ord kom hurtigere og hurtigere og mere og mere utydelige. »Du troede!... Slyngler! Kæltringer!... Jeg skal lære dig at tænke!« og han løftede sin stok, svang den og ville have ramt Alpatytj (forvalteren), hvis denne ikke instinktivt havde undveget slaget. »Troede... Kæltringer!« råbte fyrsten hastigt.

Men skønt Alpatytj, forskrækket over sin egen dristighed i at undvige slaget, nærmede sig fyrsten med bøjet, skaldet hoved i underdanighed — eller måske netop derfor — løftede fyrsten, selvom han fortsatte med at råbe: »Kæltringer!... Kast sneen tilbage på vejen!« ikke sin stok igen, men skyndte sig ind i huset.

Inden middag stod fyrstinde Marja og frøken Bourienne, der vidste, at fyrsten var i dårligt humør, og ventede på ham; frøken Bourienne med et strålende ansigt, der sagde: »Jeg ved intet, jeg er den samme som altid,« og fyrstinde Marja bleg, forskrækket og med sænkede øjne. Det sværeste for hende at bære var at vide, at hun ved sådanne lejligheder burde opføre sig som frøken Bourienne, men ikke kunne. Hun tænkte: »Hvis jeg lader, som om jeg ikke mærker noget, vil han tro, at jeg ikke har medfølelse med ham; hvis jeg virker bedrøvet og nedtrykt, vil han sige (som han har gjort før), at jeg hænger med næbbet.«
Fyrsten kiggede på datterens forskræmte ansigt og fnøs.
»Fjols... eller dukke!« mumlede han.
»Og den anden er her ikke. De har sladret,« tænkte han — og tænkte på den lille fyrstinde, der ikke var i spisestuen.
»Hvor er fyrstinden?« spurgte han. »Gemmer hun sig?«
»Hun er ikke helt rask,« svarede frøken Bourienne med et lyst smil, »så hun kommer ikke ned. Det er naturligt i hendes tilstand.«
»Hm! Hm!« mumlede fyrsten og satte sig.

Hans tallerken syntes ham ikke helt ren, og han pegede på en plet og smed den fra sig. Tikhon greb den og gav den til en lakaj. Den lille fyrstinde var ikke utilpas, men havde en så overvældende frygt for fyrsten, at hun, da hun hørte, han var i dårligt humør, havde besluttet ikke at vise sig.
»Jeg er bange for barnet,« sagde hun til frøken Bourienne. »Himlen véd, hvad en forskrækkelse kan gøre.«

I det hele taget levede den lille fyrstinde på Lysye Gory i stadig frygt og med en følelse af antipati over for den gamle fyrste, som hun ikke var klar over, fordi frygten var så meget den stærkeste følelse. Fyrsten gengældte denne antipati, men den blev overdøvet af hans foragt for hende. Da den lille fyrstinde havde vænnet sig til livet på Lysye Gory, fattede hun en særlig forkærlighed for frøken Bourienne, tilbragte hele dage med hende, bad hende sove i sit værelse og talte ofte med hende om den gamle fyrste og kritiserede ham.

»Så vi får altså besøg, mon prince?« bemærkede frøken Bourienne, idet hun foldede sin hvide serviet ud med sine rosenrøde fingre. »Hans Excellence fyrst Vasilij Kuragin og hans søn, forstår jeg?« spurgte hun med et spørgende blik.

»Hm! — hans excellence er en hundehvalp... Jeg skaffede ham hans stilling i tjenesten,« sagde fyrsten foragteligt. »Hvorfor hans søn kommer, forstår jeg ikke. Måske fyrstinde Elisabeth og fyrstinde Marja ved det. Jeg ønsker ham ikke.« (Han kiggede på sin rødmende datter.) »Er du utilpas i dag? Hva'? Bange for 'ministeren', som den idiot Alpatytj kaldte ham i morges?«
»Nej, mon père.«

Skønt frøken Bourienne havde været så uheldig i sit valg af emne, holdt hun ikke op med at tale, men snakkede videre om drivhusene og en blomst, der netop var sprunget ud, og efter suppen blev fyrsten mere omgængelig.
Efter middag gik han ind til sin svigerdatter. Den lille fyrstinde sad ved et lille bord og snakkede med Masja, sin kammerpige. Hun blev bleg, da hun så sin svigerfar.
Hun var meget forandret. Nu var hun snarere grim end smuk. Hendes kinder var indfaldne, hendes overlæbe var trukket op, og hendes øjne var dragne nedad.
»Ja, jeg føler en slags tryk,« sagde hun som svar på fyrstens spørgsmål om, hvordan hun havde det.
»Har du brug for noget?«
»Nej, merci, mon père.«
»Nå, godt, godt.«
Han forlod værelset og gik ind i forværelset, hvor Alpatytj stod med bøjet hoved.
»Er sneen kastet tilbage?«
»Ja, Deres excellence. Tilgiv mig for himlens skyld... Det var kun min dumhed.«
»Godt, godt,« afbrød fyrsten, og idet han lo på sin unaturlige vis, strakte han hånden ud, for at Alpatytj kunne kysse den, og gik derpå videre til sit arbejdsværelse.
Fyrst Vasilij ankom om aftenen. Han blev mødt i alléen af kusken og tjenere, der med højlydte råb trak hans slæder op til en af fløjene over den vej, der med vilje var dækket af sne.
Fyrst Vasilij og Anatole fik tildelt hvert sit værelse.

Anatole satte sig, efter at have taget sin overfrakke af, med armene i siden foran et bord og fæstnede sit store, smukke blik smilende og fraværende på et hjørne af det. Han betragtede hele sit liv som en uafbrudt række af fornøjelser, som nogen af en eller anden grund skulle sørge for at stille til rådighed for ham. Og dette besøg hos en gnaven gammel mand og en rig, grim arving betragtede han på samme måde. Alt dette kunne, mente han, godt forme sig morsomt og fornøjeligt. »Og hvorfor ikke gifte sig med hende, hvis hun virkelig har så mange penge? Det skader aldrig,« tænkte Anatole.

Han barberede sig og parfumerede sig med den omhu og elegance, der var ham vane, og med sit flotte hoved højt hævet gik han ind i sin fars værelse med den glade, sejrrige mine, der var ham naturlig. Fyrst Vasilijs to kammerherrer var i gang med at klæde ham på, og han så rundt med stor livlighed og nikkede muntert til sønnen, da denne trådte ind, som ville han sige: »Ja, sådan vil jeg have, du ser ud.«
»Hør, far, uden spøg — er hun meget grim?« spurgte Anatole, som om han fortsatte en samtale, de ofte havde ført under rejsen.
»Nok af det! Hvilket vrøvl! Frem for alt — prøv at være respektfuld og forsigtig over for den gamle fyrste.«
»Hvis han begynder at lave ballade, tager jeg af sted,« sagde fyrst Anatole. »Jeg kan ikke udstå de gamle mænd! Hva'?«
»Husk, at alt afhænger af dette for dig.«

I mellemtiden var det ikke blot i kammerpigerummene, at ministerens og hans søns ankomst var blevet kendt, men begges udseende var blevet minutiøst beskrevet. Fyrstinde Marja sad alene på sit værelse og forsøgte forgæves at beherske sin ophidselse.

»Hvorfor skrev de, hvorfor fortalte Lise mig det? Det kan aldrig ske!« sagde hun og kiggede på sig selv i spejlet. »Hvordan skal jeg træde ind i salonen? Selv om jeg kan lide ham, kan jeg ikke være mig selv i hans nærhed.« Alene tanken om faderens blik fyldte hende med rædsel. Den lille fyrstinde og frøken Bourienne havde allerede fra Masja, kammerpigen, modtaget den nødvendige beretning om, hvor smuk ministerens søn var, med sine rosenrøde kinder og mørke bryn, og med hvilken besvær faderen havde slæbt sine ben op ad trappen, mens sønnen var fulgt ham som en ørn, tre trin ad gangen. Med denne viden var den lille fyrstinde og frøken Bourienne, hvis livlige stemmer havde lydt fra gangen, gået ind til fyrstinde Marja.
»De er kommet, Marie,« sagde den lille fyrstinde, der kom vaklende ind og tungt sank ned i en lænestol.

Hun var ikke længere i den løse kjole, hun sædvanligvis bar om morgenen, men havde en af sine bedste kjoler på. Hendes hår var omhyggeligt sat, og hendes ansigt var livligt, hvilket dog ikke skjulte dets indfaldne og blege konturer. Klædt som hun plejede i petersborgsk selskab, var det endnu tydeligere, hvor meget grimmere hun var blevet. Også frøken Bouriennes dragt havde fået et umærkeligt tilsæt, der gjorde hendes friske, kønne ansigt endnu mere tiltalende.
»Hvad! Vil De blive siddende, som De er, kære fyrstinde?« begyndte hun. »De melder straks, at herrerne er i salonen, og vi er nødt til at gå ned, og De har slet ikke pyntet Dem!«

Den lille fyrstinde rejste sig, ringede på kammerpigen og begyndte hastigt og muntert at udtænke og gennemføre en plan for, hvordan fyrstinde Marja skulle klædes på. Fyrstinde Marjas selvfølelse blev såret af den kendsgerning, at en bejlers ankomst bragte hende i ophidselse, og endnu mere af at hendes to ledsagerinder ikke havde den fjerneste forestilling om, at det kunne være anderledes. At fortælle dem, at hun skammede sig for sig selv og for dem, ville være at røbe sin uro; mens det at afvise deres tilbud om at klæde hende ville forlænge deres erteri og insisteren. Hun rødmede, hendes smukke øjne blev matte, røde pletter viste sig på hendes ansigt, og det antog det utiltalende, martyr-agtige udtryk, som det så ofte bar, da hun underkastede sig frøken Bouriennes og Lises behandling. Begge kvinder forsøgte i fuld oprigtighed at gøre hende smuk. Hun var så grim, at ingen af dem kunne tænke på hende som en rival, og de gav sig derfor til at klæde hende på med den fuldkomne oprigtighed og faste overbevisning, kvinder nærer om, at kjoler kan gøre et ansigt smukt.

»Nej virkelig, min kære, den kjole er ikke køn,« sagde Lise og kiggede på fyrstinde Marja fra en vis afstand. »De har en kastanjebrun kjole — lad den hente. Virkelig! Det kan være, hele Deres livs skæbne står på spil. Men den her er for lys, den klæder Dem ikke!«

Det var ikke kjolen, men ansigtet og hele skikkelsen af fyrstinde Marja, der ikke var køn, men det indså hverken frøken Bourienne eller den lille fyrstinde; de troede stadig, at hvis et blåt bånd blev sat i håret, håret kammet op og det blå sjal lagt lavere på den bedste kastanjebrune kjole — og så videre — ville alt være godt. De glemte, at det bange ansigt og figuren ikke kunne ændres, og at uanset hvordan de skiftede ramme og pynt for det ansigt, ville det stadig forblive ynkeligt og grimt. Efter to-tre ombytninger, som fyrstinde Marja føjeligt underkastede sig — netop som hendes hår var sat op på hovedet (en frisure, der fuldstændig ændrede og ødelagde hendes udseende), og hun havde fået den kastanjebrune kjole på med et lysblåt sjal — gik den lille fyrstinde to gange rundt om hende, nu rettende en fold i kjolen med sin lille hånd, nu ordnende sjalet, og kiggede med hovedet bøjet til den ene side og så den anden.

»Nej, det går ikke,« sagde hun bestemt og slog hænderne sammen. »Nej, Marie, den kjole klæder Dem virkelig ikke. Jeg foretrækker Dem i Deres lille grå hverdagskjole. Gør det nu for min skyld. Katie,« sagde hun til kammerpigen, »bring fyrstinden hendes grå kjole, og De skal se, frøken Bourienne, hvordan jeg ordner det,« tilføjede hun med et smil, der varslede kunstnerisk nydelse.

Men da Katie bragte den ønskede kjole, blev fyrstinde Marja siddende ubevægelig foran spejlet, stirrende på sit ansigt, og i spejlet så hun sine øjne fulde af tårer og sin mund, der skælvede og var parat til at briste i gråd.
»Kom nu, kære fyrstinde,« sagde frøken Bourienne, »bare én lille indsats mere.«
Den lille fyrstinde tog kjolen fra kammerpigen og gik hen til fyrstinde Marja.
»Nå, nu ordner vi noget helt enkelt og klædeligt,« sagde hun.
De tre stemmer — hendes, frøken Bouriennes og Katies, der lo af noget — blandede sig i en munter lyd som fugles kvidder.
»Nej, lad mig være,« sagde fyrstinde Marja.

Hendes stemme lød så alvorlig og så bedrøvet, at fuglekvidret forstummede med det samme. De kiggede på de smukke, store, tankefulde øjne, fulde af tårer og af tanker, der så strålende og bønfaldende på dem, og forstod, at det var nyttesløst og endda grusomt at insistere.

»Skift i det mindste frisure,« sagde den lille fyrstinde. »Sagde jeg det ikke?« vendte hun sig bebrejdende mod frøken Bourienne. »Maries ansigt passer slet ikke til den frisure. Slet ikke! Lav den om.«
»Lad mig være, lad mig bare være! Det er mig fuldstændig lige meget,« svarede en stemme, der kæmpede med tårer.

Frøken Bourienne og den lille fyrstinde måtte indrømme over for sig selv, at fyrstinde Marja i den opsætning så meget grim ud, værre end sædvanligt, men det var for sent. Hun kiggede på dem med et udtryk, de begge kendte, et tankefuldt og bedrøvet udtryk. Det udtryk i fyrstinde Marjas ansigt skræmte dem ikke (hun indgød aldrig nogen frygt), men de vidste, at når det viste sig, blev hun tavs og var ikke til at rokke i sin beslutning.
»De laver det vel om?« sagde Lise. Og da fyrstinde Marja ikke svarede, forlod hun værelset.

Fyrstinde Marja blev alene. Hun rettede sig ikke efter Lises anmodning — hun lod ikke blot sit hår være, som det var, men kiggede ikke engang i spejlet. Med slappe arme sad hun med sænkede øjne og grundede. En ægtemand, en mand, et stærkt, dominerende og vidunderligt tiltrækkende væsen rejste sig i hendes fantasi og bar hende ind i en helt anden, lykkelig verden. Hun forestillede sig et barn, hendes eget — som det, hun dagen før havde set i armene på ammens datter — ved sit eget bryst, ægtemanden der stod ved siden af og kærligt betragtede hende og barnet. »Men nej, det er umuligt, jeg er for grim,« tænkte hun.
»Fyrstinden bedes komme til te. Fyrsten kommer om et øjeblik,« lød kammerpigens stemme fra døren.

Hun rettede sig op og blev skræmt over, hvad hun havde tænkt, og inden hun gik ned, gik hun ind i det rum, hvor ikonerne hang, og med blikket fæstnet på det mørke ansigt af et stort billede af Frelseren, oplyst af en lampe, stod hun foran det med foldede hænder i nogle øjeblikke. En pinefuld tvivl fyldte hendes sjæl. Kunne glæden ved kærlighed, jordisk kærlighed til en mand, være for hende? I sine tanker om ægteskab drømte fyrstinde Marja om lykke og om børn, men hendes stærkeste, mest dybt skjulte længsel var længslen efter jordisk kærlighed. Jo mere hun forsøgte at skjule denne følelse for andre og endda for sig selv, desto stærkere voksede den. »Åh, Gud,« sagde hun, »hvordan skal jeg kvæle disse djævelens fristelser i mit hjerte? Hvordan skal jeg for evigt forsage disse syndige fantasier for i fred at opfylde Din vilje?« Og næppe havde hun stillet det spørgsmål, før Gud gav hende svaret i hendes eget hjerte. »Ønsk intet for dig selv, søg intet, vær ikke bange eller misundelig. Menneskets fremtid og din egen skæbne skal forblive skjult for dig, men lev, så du er rede til alt. Hvis det er Guds vilje at prøve dig med ægteskabets pligter, vær da rede til at opfylde Hans vilje.« Med denne trøstende tanke (men dog med et håb om opfyldelsen af sin forbudte jordiske længsel) sukkede fyrstinde Marja, korsede sig og gik ned ad trappen — uden at tænke hverken på sin kjole og frisure eller på, hvordan hun skulle gå ind, eller hvad hun ville sige. Hvad betød alt det i sammenligning med Guds vilje, uden hvis forsyn ikke et hår kan falde af et menneskes hoved?

english.title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter 3
paragraphs: Old Prince Bolkonsky received a letter from Prince Vasili in November 1805, announcing that he and his son would be visiting. 'I'm going on an inspection tour, and of course I won't mind an extra seventy miles to see you, my esteemed benefactor,' wrote Prince Vasili. 'My son Anatole is traveling with me on his way to the army, so I hope you'll allow him to personally express the deep respect that, following his father's example, he feels for you.'
"It seems we won't need to introduce Mary to society—suitors are coming to us on their own," the little princess carelessly remarked upon hearing the news.
Prince Bolkonsky frowned but said nothing.
Two weeks after the letter, Prince Vasili's servants arrived one evening ahead of him, and he and his son came the next day.

Old Bolkonsky had always had a low opinion of Prince Vasili's character, and even more so recently, since under Paul and Alexander, Prince Vasili had risen to high positions and honors. Now, from the hints in his letter and from the little princess's comments, he saw where this was heading, and his low opinion turned to contemptuous hostility. He snorted whenever Prince Vasili's name came up. On the day of the visit, the old prince was especially irritable and out of sorts. Whether he was in a bad mood because Prince Vasili was coming, or whether his bad mood made the visit especially annoying, he was difficult. That morning, Tikhon had already warned the architect not to go to the prince with his report.
"Hear how he's walking?" said Tikhon, drawing the architect's attention to the sound of the prince's footsteps. "Flat on his heels—we know what that means..."

Still, at nine o'clock, the prince put on his velvet coat with a sable collar and cap and went out for his usual walk. It had snowed the day before, and the path to the greenhouse that the prince always took had been swept clean. The marks of the broom were still visible in the snow, and a shovel had been left stuck in one of the snowbanks lining both sides of the path. The prince walked through the conservatories, the servants' quarters, and the outbuildings, frowning and silent.
"Can a sleigh get through?" he asked his steward, a dignified man who resembled his master in manner and appearance, as they walked back toward the house.
"The snow is deep. I'm having the drive swept, your honor."
The prince nodded and went up to the porch. 'Thank God,' thought the steward, 'the storm has passed!'
"It would have been hard to drive up, your honor," the steward added. "I heard that a minister is coming to visit, your honor."
The prince spun around and fixed his eyes on the steward, frowning.

"What? A minister? What minister? Who gave those orders?" he snapped in his shrill, harsh voice. "The road isn't swept for my daughter the princess, but for a minister! For me, there are no ministers!"
"Your honor, I thought—"

"You thought!" the prince shouted, his words coming faster and more garbled. "You thought!... Scoundrels! Idiots!... I'll teach you to think!" And he raised his walking stick and would have struck Alpatych, the steward, if the man hadn't instinctively jumped back. "Thought... Idiots..." the prince shouted.

But although Alpatych, frightened by his own boldness in dodging the blow, stepped forward with his bald head bowed submissively—or perhaps for that very reason—the prince, though he kept shouting "Idiots! Throw the snow back on the road!" didn't raise his stick again and hurried into the house.

Before dinner, Princess Mary and Mademoiselle Bourienne, who knew the prince was in a bad mood, stood waiting for him. Mademoiselle Bourienne had a bright expression that said, 'I know nothing, I'm the same as always,' while Princess Mary was pale, frightened, with downcast eyes. What she found hardest to bear was knowing that at times like these she should act like Mademoiselle Bourienne, but couldn't. She thought: 'If I act as if nothing's wrong, he'll think I don't care. But if I look sad and gloomy, he'll say—as he has before—that I'm sulking.'
The prince looked at his daughter's frightened face and snorted.
"Fool... or dunce!" he muttered.
"And the other one isn't here either. They've been gossiping," he thought, referring to the little princess, who wasn't in the dining room.
"Where is the princess?" he asked. "Hiding?"
"She isn't feeling well," Mademoiselle Bourienne answered with a bright smile. "She won't be coming down. It's natural in her condition."
"Hm! Hm!" the prince muttered, sitting down.

His plate seemed not quite clean to him. Pointing at a spot, he flung it away. Tikhon caught it and passed it to a footman. The little princess wasn't actually ill, but she was so terrified of the prince that, hearing he was in a bad temper, she had decided not to come down.
"I'm worried about the baby," she told Mademoiselle Bourienne. "Who knows what a fright could do."

In general, life at Bald Hills meant constant fear for the little princess, mixed with a feeling of dislike for the old prince that she didn't acknowledge because the fear was so much stronger. The prince returned that dislike, but it was overwhelmed by his contempt for her. Once the little princess had settled in at Bald Hills, she took a particular liking to Mademoiselle Bourienne, spent whole days with her, asked her to sleep in her room, and often talked with her about the old prince, criticizing him.

"So we're going to have visitors, Prince?" said Mademoiselle Bourienne, unfolding her white napkin with her pink fingers. "His Excellency Prince Vasili Kuragin and his son, I understand?" she said, as if asking for confirmation.

"Hm—his excellency is a lightweight... I got him his position," the prince said dismissively. "Why his son is coming, I have no idea. Maybe Princess Elizabeth and Princess Mary know. I don't want him." He looked at his blushing daughter. "Are you unwell today? Eh? Scared of the 'minister,' as that fool Alpatych called him this morning?"
"No, Father."

Although Mademoiselle Bourienne had chosen her topic poorly, she didn't stop talking. She chattered about the conservatories and a flower that had just bloomed. After the soup, the prince became more pleasant.
After dinner he went to visit his daughter-in-law. The little princess was sitting at a small table chatting with Masha, her maid. She turned pale when she saw her father-in-law.
She had changed a great deal. She was now plain rather than pretty. Her cheeks had hollowed, her lip curled up, and her eyes were drawn down.
"Yes, I feel some pressure," she said in answer to the prince's question about how she was feeling.
"Do you need anything?"
"No, thank you, Father."
"Very well then."
He left the room and went to the vestibule, where Alpatych stood with his head bowed.
"Was the snow put back?"
"Yes, your excellency. Forgive me, for heaven's sake... It was just my stupidity."
"Fine, fine," the prince interrupted, and with his strange, forced laugh, he held out his hand for Alpatych to kiss, then went to his study.

Prince Vasili arrived that evening. He was met on the drive by coachmen and servants who, shouting loudly, dragged his sleighs up to one of the lodges over the road that had been deliberately piled with snow.
Prince Vasili and Anatole were given separate rooms.

Anatole, having taken off his coat, sat with arms crossed before a table, smilingly and absent-mindedly fixing his large, handsome eyes on one corner. He viewed his entire life as one continuous round of entertainment that someone, for some reason, had to provide for him. He regarded this visit to a grumpy old man and a rich, ugly heiress the same way. It might all turn out quite nicely and amusingly. 'And why not marry her if she really has that much money? That never hurts,' thought Anatole.

He shaved and perfumed himself with the care and elegance that had become second nature, and with his handsome head held high, entered his father's room with his naturally cheerful and confident air. Prince Vasili's two valets were busy dressing him. He looked around with great animation and gave his son a friendly nod as he entered, as if to say: 'Yes, that's exactly how I want you to look.'
"Seriously though, Father, is she really that ugly?" Anatole asked, as if picking up a conversation they'd had many times on the journey.
"Enough! Don't be ridiculous! Above all, try to be respectful and careful with the old prince."
"If he starts making trouble, I'm leaving," said Anatole. "I can't stand those old men! Right?"
"Remember, everything depends on this for you."

Meanwhile, it wasn't just the servants who knew the minister and his son had arrived—both their appearances had been described in minute detail. Princess Mary sat alone in her room, trying in vain to calm her anxiety.

"Why did they write? Why did Lise tell me about it? It can never happen!" she said, looking at herself in the mirror. "How will I walk into the drawing room? Even if I like him, I can't be myself with him now." The mere thought of her father's look filled her with dread. The little princess and Mademoiselle Bourienne had already received from Masha, the lady's maid, a thorough report on how handsome the minister's son was, with his rosy cheeks and dark eyebrows, and how his father had barely managed to drag his legs upstairs while the son had bounded up like an eagle, three steps at a time. With this intelligence in hand, the little princess and Mademoiselle Bourienne, whose chattering voices had been audible from the hallway, went into Princess Mary's room.
"Did you know they've arrived, Marie?" said the little princess, waddling in and sinking heavily into an armchair.

She had changed out of her usual loose morning gown and put on one of her best dresses. Her hair was done up and her face was lively—though this couldn't hide how much thinner and paler she had become. Dressed as she used to be in Petersburg society, it was even more obvious how much plainer she looked now. Some subtle touch had been added to Mademoiselle Bourienne's outfit that made her fresh, pretty face even more appealing.

"What—are you going to stay like that, dear princess?" she began. "They're going to announce the gentlemen in the drawing room any minute and we'll have to go down, and you haven't done anything with yourself!"

The little princess jumped up, rang for the maid, and with cheerful energy began planning how to dress Princess Mary. Princess Mary's pride was wounded by the fact that a suitor's arrival excited her, and even more by her companions' complete inability to imagine she might feel differently about it. To tell them she was embarrassed—for herself and for them—would be to reveal her agitation. To refuse their help would only prolong their teasing and insistence. She blushed, her beautiful eyes dimmed, red blotches appeared on her face, and it took on the unattractive, long-suffering expression it so often wore as she submitted to Mademoiselle Bourienne and Lise. Both women sincerely tried to make her pretty. She was so plain that neither could see her as a rival, so they set about dressing her with genuine conviction—the unshakable female belief that clothes can make any face pretty.

"No, really, dear, this dress won't do," said Lise, studying Princess Mary from a distance. "You have a maroon dress—go get it. Seriously! Your whole life might depend on this. But this one is too light, it's not right for you!"

It wasn't the dress but Princess Mary's face and whole figure that weren't attractive. But neither Mademoiselle Bourienne nor the little princess could see this. They still believed that if a blue ribbon were placed in her hair, the hair pinned up, and the blue scarf lowered on the best maroon dress, everything would be fine. They forgot that the anxious face and the figure couldn't be changed, and that no matter how much they altered the setting and accessories around that face, it would still look sad and plain. After two or three outfit changes—to which Princess Mary meekly submitted—once her hair had been piled on top of her head (a style that completely altered and worsened her appearance) and she had put on a maroon dress with a pale-blue scarf, the little princess circled her twice, adjusting a fold here, straightening the scarf there, tilting her head this way and that.

"No, it won't work," she said firmly, clasping her hands. "No, Marie, this dress really doesn't suit you. I prefer you in your little gray everyday dress. Please, do it for my sake. Katie," she called to the maid, "bring the princess her gray dress, and you'll see, Mademoiselle Bourienne, how I'll fix it up." She smiled with the anticipated pleasure of an artist.

But when Katie brought the gray dress, Princess Mary sat motionless before the mirror, staring at her face. In the reflection she could see her eyes filling with tears and her mouth quivering, about to burst into sobs.
"Come, dear princess," said Mademoiselle Bourienne, "just one more little effort."
The little princess took the dress from the maid and came over to Princess Mary.
"Now we'll make something simple and flattering," she said.
The three voices—hers, Mademoiselle Bourienne's, and Katie's, who was laughing at something—blended together in a cheerful sound, like birdsong.
"No, leave me alone," said Princess Mary.

Her voice sounded so serious and so sad that the birdsong stopped at once. They looked at her beautiful, large, thoughtful eyes, shining with tears and unspoken thoughts, gazing imploringly at them—and understood that insisting would be useless, even cruel.

"At least change your hairstyle," said the little princess. "Didn't I tell you," she added, turning reproachfully to Mademoiselle Bourienne, "that Mary's face doesn't suit that style at all? Not at all! Please change it."
"Leave me alone, please leave me alone! It's all the same to me," answered a voice struggling with tears.

Mademoiselle Bourienne and the little princess had to admit to themselves that Princess Mary looked very plain like this—worse than usual—but it was too late. She gazed at them with an expression they both knew well: thoughtful and sad. This look never frightened anyone (she was never intimidating), but they knew that when it appeared, she became silent and nothing could change her mind.
"You will change it, won't you?" said Lise. When Princess Mary didn't answer, she left the room.

Princess Mary was left alone. She didn't do as Lise asked; she not only kept her hair as it was but didn't even glance in the mirror. Letting her arms fall helplessly, she sat with downcast eyes and lost herself in thought. In her imagination, a husband appeared—a man, strong, commanding, and strangely attractive—and carried her away into a completely different, happy world. She imagined a child, her own—like the one she had seen yesterday in her nurse's daughter's arms—at her breast, with the husband standing beside her, gazing tenderly at her and the baby. 'But no, it's impossible—I'm too ugly,' she thought.
"Please come to tea. The prince will be out in a moment," came the maid's voice from the door.

She stirred and was appalled at what she had been thinking. Before going downstairs, she went into the room where the icons hung and stood before the dark face of a large icon of the Savior, lit by a lamp, her hands folded in prayer. A painful doubt filled her soul. Could the joy of love—earthly love for a man—really be meant for her? In her dreams of marriage, Princess Mary imagined happiness and children, but her deepest, most hidden longing was for earthly love. The harder she tried to conceal this feeling from others and from herself, the stronger it grew. 'Oh God,' she said, 'how can I overcome these temptations? How can I give up these sinful dreams and peacefully fulfill Your will?' And as soon as she asked the question, God answered in her own heart. 'Desire nothing for yourself. Seek nothing. Be not anxious or envious. The future—both mankind's and your own—must remain hidden from you. But live so that you are ready for anything. If God wills that you be tested in marriage, be ready to fulfill His will.' With this comforting thought—though still harboring hope for the fulfillment of her forbidden earthly longing—Princess Mary sighed, crossed herself, and went downstairs, thinking not of her dress or hairstyle or how she would enter or what she would say. What did any of that matter compared to the will of God, without whose care not a single hair falls from anyone's head?
